title: Comparative assessment of ensemble and machine learning models for susceptibility mapping of 2024 Wushi earthquake-triggered landslides
content:
by Yutong Wu, Junpeng Huang, Wenqian Li, Xiangfeng Jia, Yaning Li, Zhiyi Wang

Coseismic landslide susceptibility mapping plays a critical role in disaster risk mitigation, infrastructure protection, and territorial spatial planning, particularly in tectonically active mountain belts such as the Tianshan Mountains. Conventional machine learning models often suffer from overfitting and inadequate generalization capability due to their homogeneous structures and inflexible modeling strategies. In this study, targeting the coseismic landslides triggered by the 2024 Ms 7.1 Wushi earthquake in the Biedieli River basin, a landslide inventory comprising 904 events was compiled and randomly partitioned into training (70%) and validation (30%) datasets. Nine conditioning factors pertaining to topography, geology, environment, and seismicity were selected, including elevation, slope angle, slope aspect, curvature, lithology, distance to faults, distance to rivers, distance to roads, and peak ground acceleration (PGA). The predictive performance of an ensemble learning model, LightGBM, was compared against three benchmark machine learning models, i.e., artificial neural network (ANN), decision tree (DT), and naive Bayes (NB). Multicollinearity diagnosis and factor importance ranking were conducted using variance inflation factor (VIF) and correlation attribute evaluation (CAE), respectively. The model performance was validated and compared via the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) and several statistical metrics including accuracy and F1-score. The results indicate that elevation (AM = 0.6296), PGA (AM = 0.5810), and distance to roads (AM = 0.4934) are the primary determinants of landslide occurrence. The LightGBM model achieved the best overall predictive performance on the validation dataset, with an AUC of 0.961 and the highest accuracy (0.890) and F1-score (0.895), followed by ANN (AUC = 0.957, accuracy = 0.876, F1-score = 0.876), DT (AUC = 0.947, accuracy = 0.856, F1-score = 0.860), and NB (AUC = 0.919, accuracy = 0.862, F1-score = 0.869). From the training dataset to the validation dataset, the AUC decay of LightGBM was merely 2.6%, indicating good generalization capability. The high and very high susceptibility zones account for 10.51% to 19.43% of the study area across the four models, predominantly concentrated in the mid-elevation valley zones (2036.5–2959 m), steep slopes exceeding 40°, areas with PGA greater than 0.48 g, and the vicinity of the Maidan fault zone. The susceptibility maps produced in this study can provide a scientific basis for post-earthquake emergency response, hazard risk assessment, and disaster mitigation in the Tianshan seismic belt.
